title: Small request CPU fanout and shared buffer postmortem
content:
Summary:

This is a postmortem and working notes for recurring small-request latency spikes observed in the hosted API where payloads are ~50-200 bytes (metadata-heavy requests, short prompts). Incidents began to surface in late August and manifested as 95th/99th percentile tail latency regressions on CPU-heavy frontends that perform tokenization and request decoding before handing off to GPU inference. The goal of this doc is to capture root-cause evidence, experiments we ran, and concrete mitigation + follow-ups.

Symptoms observed:
- Sudden increases in 95th/99th latency for requests under 100ms median, typically only affecting small-payload routes.
- Correlated CPU utilization spikes on the request-parsing workers (not GPU).
- Spikes occur in bursts (hundreds of requests over ~30–90s) and then subside. Not correlated to model changes.
- Evidence of increased syscalls per request and context-switch counts during spikes.

Hypothesis summary (what we tested):
1) Small requests hit an unfavorable code path that does more per-request syscalls and allocations (parse JSON headers, decompress, tokenization warmup).
2) Worker threadpool/affinity causes fanout where a single incoming burst wakes many threads, causing lock contention on a shared buffer pool and kernel scheduling thrash.
3) Python interpreter overhead (GIL handoffs and per-request heap churn) amplifies the above for our Python-based preproc.

Reproduction steps (local microbench):
- Synthetic client sending 1k requests/s of 80–120 byte JSON payloads to the small-payload route.
- Enabled detailed tracing: per-request timestamps, getrusage snapshots, and eBPF capture of epoll_wait/read/write pairs.
- Collected flamegraphs for user+kernel at 10ms sampling.

Key profiling findings (evidence):
- Flamegraphs show two consistent hotspots: JSON parsing and tokenize_normalize_unicode (tokenizer). Tokenizer shows many short allocations and fast loops in C extension, but lots of Python->C boundary crossings.
- Syscall trace: many read()/recv() + epoll_wait cycles per request; apparent underutilization of batched reads when requests are small and interleaved.
- Scheduler traces: burst arrival causes N threads to be runnable simultaneously; kernel schedules them in rounds, producing small slices and high context-switch counts.
- Lock contention: a shared small-buffer allocator (bytearray reuse pool) guarded by a single mutex shows heavy contention during spikes; contention appears in stack traces near buffer_pool.acquire() and in the C tokenizer entry.
- GIL behavior: when tokenization moves into C, GIL is released for parts, but Python-side orchestration still requires frequent GIL reacquisitions to manage per-request metadata objects, increasing latency variance.

Quantitative numbers (representative):
- Median P95 before mitigations: 180ms. After initial mitigation (buffer pool sharding): P95 ~95ms.
- Context-switches per 10k requests during spike: 85k -> 32k after sharding.
- Syscalls per request: median 6, spike tail 18.

What we tried (short experiments & outcomes):
1) Buffer pool sharding: replaced single global buffer_pool mutex with 8 shard buckets keyed by thread id. Outcome: reduced lock contention; improved tail by ~45%. Low-risk config change, rolled to canary.
2) Tokenizer warm process: pre-warmed tokenizer instances and pre-populated internal caches on worker start. Outcome: small improvement for first N requests, but did not remove tail spikes.
3) Read batching at socket layer: introduced a short (200us) aggregation window in the acceptor that coalesced reads into a single batch. Outcome: reduced syscalls per request but increased median by ~6ms; tradeoff not acceptable for low-latency routes.
4) Thread affinity changes: pinned worker pools to separate CPUs to reduce cross-core wakeups. Outcome: slight improvement in jitter but operationally brittle on noisy noisy hosts.

Root causes (consolidated):
- Contention on shared small-buffer allocator (single mutex) during bursts. This was the dominant contributor to kernel waiting and context switches.
- Per-request orchestration on the Python side (object allocation + bookkeeping) leads to chattiness with the C tokenizer; repeated GIL transitions and short-lived allocations amplify tail latency for small requests.
- Socket read pattern for small interleaved requests prevented efficient batching at kernel level, causing more syscalls and epoll wake cycles.

Immediate remediation (rolled / recommended):
- Shard the small-buffer pool by default (rolled to canary and then all workers). This is the low-effort, high-impact fix.
- Increase worker-side preallocated metadata objects for small routes (object pools) to reduce per-request allocation pressure.
- Keep the short read-aggregation experiment in a config flag; do not enable globally.

Medium-term work (backlog tickets):
- ENG-RTC-2102: Reimplement small-buffer allocator in C with lock-free per-thread caches and explicit fallback to shared slab. Target: 3–4 weeks engineering.
- ENG-RTC-2103: Move tokenization orchestration into a C-native worker for small-payload path (reduce Python roundtrips). Target: prototype 6 weeks.
- ENG-RTC-2104: Evaluate zero-copy JSON parsing for header-only requests; reduce allocations and copies.
- ENG-RTC-2105: Socket layer optimization: adaptive batching based on observed RPS and latency SLO; dynamic micro-window with per-route thresholds.

Operational notes / runbook additions:
- Add a lightweight tail-latency alert for small-payload routes that includes context-switch and mutex-wait metrics.
- On future incidents, capture a 60s eBPF syscall trace and a lightweight scheduler trace to help decide if lock contention is present.

Open questions and unknowns:
- How much of the GIL overhead can be eliminated via moving orchestration into a C driver without introducing maintenance burden?
- Are there other shared mutexes in the hot path we have not observed due to sampling limitations?
- What's the tradeoff curve for read-aggregation across diverse customer latency SLOs?

Action items (owners & ETA):
- Aisha: finalize allocator shard rollout across all regions (done 2024-10-12).
- Jon: prototype C per-thread buffer caches and open RFC (due 2024-10-30).
- Sofia: benchmark tokenizer C-driver prototype on dedicated machines and report (due 2024-11-15).
- Evan (SRE): add runbook steps and new alert; instrument mutex wait histograms (due 2024-10-07).

Appendix (artifacts):
- flamegraphs and sampling captures archived at s3://redwood-profiles/small-req-2024-09-06/
- perf.data and BPF traces attached to JIRA-ENG-1789.

Conclusions:
Sharding the buffer pool yielded the largest immediate reduction in tail latency and was low-risk. The remaining work falls into two classes: (1) reduce Python orchestration overhead by moving hot paths closer to C and reducing GIL crossings, and (2) implement more robust per-thread memory caches and adaptive socket batching to avoid syscall and scheduling thrash for small, bursty workloads. The medium-term changes require coordination between serving-runtime, applied-ml (tokenizer owners), and SREs for rollout and validation.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally operational and contains loose experiment notes. Please add comments inline if you have reproductions or different telemetry that contradicts the contours above.
